title: The Yearbook of Maple Street
premise: Zephyrine Galloway has spent three years perfecting invisibility: raising her younger siblings while her mother works night shifts at the hospital, keeping her grades immaculate, and never once letting anyone past her locker. Then history teacher Ms. Okafor pairs her with Theo Marchetti—her nemesis since seventh grade—for a semester-long project restoring the school's forgotten 1974 yearbook, which reveals that Zephyrine's late grandmother and Theo's grandfather were best friends who founded the school's first scholarship together before a mysterious falling-out. As Zephyrine and Theo dig through archives, they uncover a buried family secret: the scholarship fund was stolen, and Zephyrine's family has been quietly paying the price for two generations. When the truth threatens to destroy both families' legacies, Zephyrine must choose between protecting her carefully managed invisibility and claiming a name worth being seen under—ending with her publicly restoring her grandmother's story, accepting the scholarship her grandmother created, and finally letting her siblings, her mother, and Theo see the whole of who she is.
about_author: Ines Blackwood grew up in a rust-belt town where the high school yearbooks were kept in a locked cabinet no one ever opened, a detail that haunted her into adulthood. She writes young adult fiction about kids who carry more than their share, and she still can't resist a story about old paper holding old secrets.

chapters.title: The Art of Not Being Noticed
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. A morning in the Galloway household: packing lunches, checking homework, getting siblings out the door before her mother's shift ends. At school, she executes her invisibility routine flawlessly—until Ms. Okafor announces semester project pairs. The emotional beat: exhaustion disguised as control, and dread when 'Marchetti' is read aloud.

chapters.title: Assigned
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo, popular and effortlessly loud, is furious at being paired with the girl who reported him in seventh grade. Their first meeting in the library is pure friction. Ms. Okafor hands them a box: the school's 1974 yearbook, damaged and forgotten, to restore and present. The beat: reluctant truce sealed by mutual dislike of failure.

chapters.title: What the Box Held
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Sorting the yearbook's water-stained pages at her kitchen table, she freezes: a photo of her grandmother, Ruth Galloway, laughing with a boy named Sal Marchetti. Her grandmother never spoke of high school. The beat: the first crack in Zephyrine's belief that her family's story is small and closed.

chapters.title: Rules of Engagement
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo notices Zephyrine flinch at the photo and starts asking questions she won't answer. Meanwhile we see his own pressure: a father who expects Marchetti men to be legends. He proposes project rules—no personal questions. The beat: two people building walls and pretending it's architecture.

chapters.title: The Scholarship Plaque
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Researching in the school archive, they find the Ruth Galloway and Salvatore Marchetti Scholarship, discontinued in 1975—one year after it was founded. The plaque's donor line has been scratched out. Zephyrine lies to Theo about why her hands are shaking. The beat: inheritance as mystery, and the cost of lying to an ally.

chapters.title: Little Witnesses
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Her younger sister Junie finds the yearbook photo and asks who the boy is; her brother Miles quietly reveals he's been skipping the free-lunch line out of shame. Zephyrine realizes her siblings are watching her invisibility and copying it. The beat: the weight of being the example, not just the caretaker.

chapters.title: Sal Marchetti Speaks
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo visits his grandfather Sal, sharp-tongued and cagey, who goes silent at the mention of Ruth Galloway and orders him out of the den. Theo, rattled, breaks his own rule and asks Zephyrine what her family did. The beat: the past pushing back, and the truce straining.

chapters.title: Detention Economics
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Zephyrine gets detention defending Junie from a bully—publicly, visibly—and the school calls her mother, who misses work to come in. Guilt and fury collide. Theo witnesses the whole scene and sees, for the first time, what Zephyrine carries. The beat: invisibility failing, and it not being the disaster she feared.

chapters.title: The 1975 Newspaper
chapters.summary: Both POVs alternating. In the library's microfilm, they find it: a 1975 article accusing Ruth Galloway of stealing the scholarship fund. No retraction. No follow-up. Zephyrine's grandmother was labeled a thief at seventeen. The beat: horror, and the dawning question—who actually took the money?

chapters.title: What Mom Knows
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Zephyrine confronts her mother, who admits she knows the family name is 'complicated,' refuses to explain, and forbids the project topic. Mother and daughter clash over whether protecting the kids means keeping secrets. The beat: love expressed as silence, and Zephyrine refusing it for the first time.

chapters.title: An Uneven Alliance
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo offers to help clear Ruth's name even though the truth might implicate Sal. Zephyrine doesn't trust it—until Theo shows her Sal's old ledger, which he found and hasn't told his father about. The beat: trust built not on words but on someone handing you evidence they could have burned.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. The ledger shows deposits to the fund that stopped in 1975—and a withdrawal signed by the school's then-principal, Ruth's mentor. The money didn't vanish into Ruth's pockets; it was taken upward. The beat: vindication and vertigo, because the principal's family still runs the town.

chapters.title: Homecoming Interference
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Homecoming week. Zephyrine can't attend—no money, no time—so Theo engineers a way for the whole Galloway crew to come, disguising it as a 'project event.' Zephyrine sees through it and is furious at the charity, then undone by how happy Junie looks. The beat: pride versus belonging, and belonging winning by a nose.

chapters.title: Ashworth's Shadow
chapters.summary: Both POVs. The principal's family name is Ashworth; the current principal, Diane Ashworth, is the granddaughter. When the kids request archive access to the 1975 financial records, Diane personally denies it and warns them off the topic. The beat: the past isn't dead—it's employed, and watching them.

chapters.title: The Falling-Out, Reconstructed
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. A retired teacher's oral-history tape reveals the truth: Sal accused Ruth of theft to protect her—because Diane's father threatened to have Ruth, the scholarship girl with no family money, expelled and prosecuted. Sal took the blame for the friendship's death. The beat: the nemesis-ship of their grandparents was a sacrifice, not a betrayal.

chapters.title: Deadline Pressure
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Ms. Okafor announces the project will be presented publicly at the school's anniversary assembly—meaning their findings go on record. Theo's father, a school board member, demands Theo drop the topic. First real fight between Theo and his dad. The beat: choosing a legacy over an inheritance.

chapters.title: The Thing About Labels
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. A classmate's cruel joke about 'thief blood' spreads; Zephyrine nearly quits the project to shield her siblings. Instead, she finds Junie has written a report for class about 'my brave great-grandma.' Zephyrine understands: the kids already believe in Ruth. The beat: shame losing to a child's faith.

chapters.title: Everything Surfaces
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Diane Ashworth, tipped off, accuses Zephyrine of stealing archive materials and threatens suspension days before the assembly. Theo publicly takes the blame, burning his own spotless record. Zephyrine, who spent years avoiding exactly this kind of spotlight, chooses to stand next to him in it. The beat: the labels coming off, on purpose.

chapters.title: The Assembly
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Climax. Before the whole school, they present the restored yearbook and the ledger: Ruth Galloway was framed; Sal Marchetti was her shield; the Ashworths took the fund. Diane denies it, but the retired teacher's tape plays, and the room turns. The beat: terror transfigured into voice—Zephyrine, the invisible girl, holding a microphone.

chapters.title: Fallout
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Consequences land: an investigation opens, Theo's father is furious, Diane is suspended pending review. Theo and Zephyrine deal with the aftermath apart, each wondering if the friendship was only ever the project. The beat: the quiet after the storm, and the fear that courage was a one-time thing.

chapters.title: What Ruth Left
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Zephyrine's mother finally opens Ruth's old sewing box: inside, a letter Ruth wrote but never sent, forgiving Sal and asking whoever found it to 'be seen, even when it costs.' The scholarship is provisionally reinstated in both names. The beat: inheritance redefined—not money, but permission.

chapters.title: The Yearbook of Maple Street
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, closing. Spring. Zephyrine signs the new yearbook—hers, with her name printed in the scholarship announcement—and lets her siblings, her mother, and Theo read the dedication she wrote to Ruth. Her locker, for once, stands open. The beat: belonging chosen, identity claimed, the invisible girl visible at last.
